title: PySpark Storage Layout — Mid Recognition Track
description: A 10-exercise mid recognition track for PySpark Storage Layout at NordGrid Energy. Five modules: SLI1 What Is Bucketing? · SLI2 Bucketing in Plans · SLI3 What Is Z-Ordering? · SLI4 When Bucketing / Z-Order Did Not Help · SLI5 Reading Mid-Level Storage Layouts.

datasets.description: Schema reference (sample rows). NordGrid Energy at mid scale; the CSV is a small sample for schema reference.

tasks.title: bucketBy(N, col) — What It Does at Write Time

description.context: BUCKETING is the second major layout-side optimization beyond partitioning. When you write df.write.bucketBy(N, 'col').sortBy('col').saveAsTable('t'), Spark hashes the column value into N buckets and writes each row to the bucket matching its hash. The number N is chosen by the engineer; common values are 50-500 for production tables. The result on disk is N parquet files (one per bucket), and a 'bucket spec' entry in the table metadata recording the bucket count and column. Bucketing is different from partitioning in two ways. First, bucket files do not produce directories — just files at the table root with predictable names like part-00037-bucketed.parquet. Second, bucketing pre-shuffles data: a downstream query that JOINS or AGGREGATES on the bucketed column can skip the shuffle entirely because matching values are already co-located in matching buckets.
description.task: What did bucketBy(50, 'customer_id') actually do here?

Row Count: 200000

fields.label: What did bucketBy(50, 'customer_id') actually do here?
options: Created 50 directories named bucket=0, bucket=1 etc., each holding one parquet file with the matching customer_ids. The bucket count is encoded in directory names.

Hashed every row's customer_id into one of 50 buckets and wrote each bucket's rows into one parquet file at the table root. The bucket spec was registered in the catalog so downstream queries can use it.
Sorted the entire table by customer_id and wrote 50 evenly-sized parquet files in customer_id order. The 50 number determines file count only; bucketing is just a synonym for repartition + sort.
Created a hash index on customer_id stored in a separate index file alongside the parquet files. The 50 indicates the index granularity (50 hash buckets per index level).
fields.correctAnswer: Hashed every row's customer_id into one of 50 buckets and wrote each bucket's rows into one parquet file at the table root. The bucket spec was registered in the catalog so downstream queries can use it.
fields.rationale: Hash distribution and catalog metadata are the two essential elements at write time. Files appear at the table root, named like part-00000-bucketed... through part-00049-bucketed... with NO column=value directories. The bucket spec (50 buckets, customer_id column) is recorded in the catalog metadata. This metadata is what enables downstream queries to skip shuffles — Spark looks at the bucket spec at plan time and recognizes that data is pre-distributed, so a join on customer_id no longer requires an Exchange. Bucketing differs from partitioning: no directories, no pruning, but does enable shuffle-skip on the bucketed column.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats bucketing as creating directories; it creates files at the root level.

Option C: Treats bucketing as sort + repartition; the catalog bucket-spec metadata is essential.

Option D: Invents an index file. Bucketing reorganizes data, not metadata indexes.

tasks.pssReference: PSI2 lesson 6 (Bucketing — write semantics), PSI3 lesson 5 (Bucketing for Shuffle Skip).

tasks.title: Bucketing vs Partitioning

description.context: Bucketing and partitioning solve different problems. Partitioning enables PRUNING — Spark skips entire directories that don't match a filter. Bucketing enables SHUFFLE SKIP — Spark recognizes pre-distributed data and avoids re-shuffling for joins/aggregations on the bucketed column. The cardinality requirements differ too. Partition columns need 10-10,000 distinct values (each becomes a directory). Bucket columns can have any cardinality — bucketBy(50, 'customer_id') with 200K customers works fine because all 200K values hash into just 50 buckets. The choice is not exclusive: a table can be BOTH partitioned (e.g., by date) AND bucketed (by customer_id) at the same time.
description.task: What is the structural difference and which optimization does each enable?

fields.label: What is the structural difference and which optimization does each enable?
options: Layout A is the production-grade layout; Layout B's flat file structure indicates a write failure. Spark normally creates partitioned output by default, so a bucket-only output without any partition columns is rarely correct.

Layout A is the production-grade layout; Layout B's flat file structure indicates a write failure. Spark normally creates partitioned output by default; bucket-only output without partition columns is rarely correct.

Layout A enables partition pruning on region (skip non-matching directories). Layout B enables shuffle-skip on customer_id joins (matching customer_ids land in matching buckets). Different layouts solve different problems.
Layout A and Layout B are mutually exclusive — a table cannot be both partitioned and bucketed at the same time. Combining requires Delta Lake; standard parquet supports one or the other only.
fields.correctAnswer: Layout A enables partition pruning on region (skip non-matching directories). Layout B enables shuffle-skip on customer_id joins (matching customer_ids land in matching buckets). Different layouts solve different problems.
fields.rationale: The two layouts target different optimizations. Layout A: directory-based partitioning means a query filtering region == 'NORTH' reads ONLY the region=NORTH/ directory — that's pruning. Layout B: bucketed files with metadata bucket spec means a query joining on customer_id can skip the shuffle because Spark knows matching customer_ids hash to matching buckets — that's shuffle skip. The cardinality constraints differ: Layout A's region has 4 values (good partition cardinality); Layout B's customer_id has 200K values (impossible partition column, fine bucket column). Standard parquet tables can be BOTH partitioned and bucketed simultaneously: e.g., partitionBy('region').bucketBy(50, 'customer_id').
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats the structural difference as cosmetic; it directly drives different optimizations.

Option B: Treats flat bucket layout as a failure; it is the expected output of bucketBy.

Option D: Treats partitioning + bucketing as exclusive; they compose. Delta is not required.

tasks.pssReference: PSI2 lessons 5-6 (Partitioning vs Bucketing — semantic differences).

tasks.title: BucketedTableScan in the Plan

description.context: When you query a bucketed table and Spark recognizes the bucket spec, the plan changes shape. Look for two signals. First, the FileScan operator becomes a BUCKETED FileScan or shows 'SelectedBucketsCount: M out of N' — proving Spark used the bucket layout. Second, when joining a bucketed table to another table on the bucketed column, the Exchange that would normally appear above the bucketed side DISAPPEARS — Spark trusts that data is already pre-distributed by the hash. The other side may still need a shuffle (unless it's also bucketed compatibly), but eliminating one side of the shuffle is significant savings.
description.task: What does this plan tell you about whether bucketing helped?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Left Table: positions (12M rows, NOT bucketed)

Right Table: customer_dim_bucketed (200K rows, bucketBy(50, 'customer_id'))

Join Key: customer_id

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Plan from a NordGrid join between a bucketed customer_dim and a non-bucketed positions table — bucket spec engages on one side

evidence.label: Plan output
evidence.content:
# Query: positions.join(customer_dim_bucketed, on='customer_id', how='inner')

== Physical Plan ==
AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false
+- ShuffledHashJoin [customer_id#0], [customer_id#50], Inner, BuildRight
   :- Exchange hashpartitioning(customer_id#0, 50)
   :  +- FileScan parquet positions [customer_id#0, daily_kw#3, region#5]
   +- FileScan parquet customer_dim_bucketed [customer_id#50, customer_type#52]
      SelectedBucketsCount: 50 out of 50
      Bucketed: true
      ⟵ NO Exchange operator above this scan

# Compare with same join if customer_dim were NOT bucketed:
#   +- Sort [customer_id ASC]
#      +- Exchange hashpartitioning(customer_id, 200)   ← extra shuffle
#         +- FileScan parquet customer_dim_unbucketed

fields.label: What does this plan tell you about whether bucketing helped?
options: Bucketing did not help — the Exchange on the positions side proves a shuffle still happened. Bucket-aware optimization only fires when BOTH sides are bucketed compatibly. Useless effort to bucket only customer_dim.

Bucketing engaged on customer_dim_bucketed (Bucketed: true, no Exchange above). The other side (positions) still needed a shuffle. The non-bucketed side's shuffle uses 50 partitions to match the bucket count — clean handoff. One shuffle eliminated of two.

The plan is misleading — Bucketed: true is informational only. The actual runtime behavior shuffles both sides regardless of what the plan operator says. Bucketing benefits only appear if you set spark.sql.bucketing.enabled=true, which is off by default in Spark 3.5+.

Bucketing engaged on both sides. The positions side appears to have an Exchange but that's actually a fast bucket-rehash done locally, not a true cross-cluster shuffle. Both reads are bucketed; both shuffles are eliminated.
fields.correctAnswer: Bucketing engaged on customer_dim_bucketed (Bucketed: true, no Exchange above). The other side (positions) still needed a shuffle. The non-bucketed side's shuffle uses 50 partitions to match the bucket count — clean handoff. One shuffle eliminated of two.
fields.rationale: The plan signals are independent of metadata claims; runtime evidence determines whether the bucket spec is honored. First, 'Bucketed: true' and 'SelectedBucketsCount: 50 out of 50' on the FileScan show Spark read the bucket layout. Second, NO Exchange operator appears above customer_dim_bucketed's FileScan — Spark trusted that data is pre-distributed. The positions side is not bucketed, so it must shuffle to align — Exchange hashpartitioning(customer_id, 50) does that, with partition count matching customer_dim's 50 buckets for clean alignment. Result: one shuffle (positions side) instead of two (both sides). When BOTH sides are bucketed compatibly, BOTH Exchanges disappear and the join runs without ANY shuffle.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats bucketing as all-or-nothing; one-sided bucketing still eliminates one shuffle.

Option C: Invents a disable-by-default flag. Bucketing is enabled by default in Spark 3.5+.

Option D: Misreads the plan; positions side has a real Exchange, not a bucket rehash.

tasks.pssReference: PSI3 lesson 5 (Bucketing for Shuffle Skip — single-side and double-side patterns).

tasks.title: Bucket Count Mismatch — Why Bucketing Did Not Help

description.context: Bucket-side shuffle skip only works when bucket counts MATCH between the two tables being joined. If table A has 50 buckets and table B has 200 buckets on the same column, Spark CANNOT skip the shuffle on either side — the hash distributions don't align (a customer_id that hashes to bucket 7 of 50 ends up in bucket 28 of 200, and Spark cannot pair them without redistributing). The plan signal: Exchange operators appear above BOTH bucketed sides, both shuffling to 200 partitions (or some other unified count). The bucket counts are visible in catalog metadata; mismatches are silent — Spark does not warn.
description.task: Why did bucketing fail to eliminate the shuffles, and what is the fix?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Left Table: positions_bucketed (bucketBy(50, 'customer_id'))

Right Table: customer_dim_bucketed (bucketBy(200, 'customer_id'))

Engineer Assumption: both bucketed → no shuffle

Actual Observation: both sides shuffle, same as if neither were bucketed

Performance Vs Unbucketed: identical (no benefit observed)

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Two bucketed tables joined together but with mismatched bucket counts (50 vs 200), so neither side benefits

evidence.label: Plan output
evidence.content:
# Catalog metadata
DESCRIBE EXTENDED positions_bucketed:
  Num Buckets: 50
  Bucket Columns: [customer_id]

DESCRIBE EXTENDED customer_dim_bucketed:
  Num Buckets: 200
  Bucket Columns: [customer_id]

# Plan for: positions_bucketed.join(customer_dim_bucketed, on='customer_id')

+- SortMergeJoin [customer_id], [customer_id], Inner
   :- Sort [customer_id ASC]
   :  +- Exchange hashpartitioning(customer_id, 200)   ← left shuffles
   :     +- FileScan parquet positions_bucketed
   +- Sort [customer_id ASC]
      +- Exchange hashpartitioning(customer_id, 200)   ← right shuffles
         +- FileScan parquet customer_dim_bucketed

fields.label: Why did bucketing fail to eliminate the shuffles, and what is the fix?
options: Bucketing only works for inner joins; the optimizer disabled bucket-skip because of the implicit isnotnull condition added by Spark for safety. Fix: explicitly cast customer_id to NOT NULL via dropna() before the join is invoked.

Bucketing only works for inner joins; the optimizer disabled bucket-skip because of the implicit isnotnull condition added by Spark for safety. Fix: explicitly cast customer_id to NOT NULL via dropna() before the join.

Both tables ARE benefiting from bucketing internally; the visible Exchanges are pre-bucketing rehash steps that Spark adds for safety. The actual shuffle volume is much smaller than the plan suggests. Fix: nothing needed.

The bucket counts (50 vs 200) don't match. Spark cannot align hash distributions across mismatched bucket counts; both sides must shuffle. Fix: rewrite both tables with the SAME bucket count (e.g., both 200) so the bucket spec aligns.
fields.correctAnswer: The bucket counts (50 vs 200) don't match. Spark cannot align hash distributions across mismatched bucket counts; both sides must shuffle. Fix: rewrite both tables with the SAME bucket count (e.g., both 200) so the bucket spec aligns.
fields.rationale: Bucket-aware shuffle skip requires identical bucket counts on the join column. With 50 vs 200 buckets, a customer_id that hashes to bucket 7 (mod 50) on the left lands in bucket X (mod 200) on the right — and the relationship between 7-mod-50 and X-mod-200 is not a 1:1 alignment Spark can use. Both sides must shuffle to a common partition count (here 200). The fix is to rewrite one table with matching bucket count: bucketBy(200, 'customer_id') on positions, OR bucketBy(50, 'customer_id') on customer_dim. Multiple-of relationships (50/200) sometimes work in newer Spark versions but the safe rule is exact match. Spark does not WARN about mismatched bucket counts — silent missed optimization.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Invents a type-mismatch issue not implied by the scenario.

Option B: Invents an inner-only or null-safety constraint. Bucketing supports outer joins.

Option C: Treats Exchange as a phantom; it is a real cross-cluster shuffle.

tasks.pssReference: PSI3 lesson 5 (Bucketing — bucket count alignment requirements).

tasks.title: OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY — Reading the Delta Log

description.context: Z-ORDERING is a Delta Lake feature that physically reorganizes file layout to co-locate rows with similar values across MULTIPLE columns. It is invoked via OPTIMIZE table ZORDER BY (col1, col2). The Z-order is a multi-dimensional space-filling curve: rows whose (col1, col2) values are close in the 2D space end up in the same parquet file. After Z-ordering, every parquet file gets min/max statistics for the Z-ordered columns; queries with range filters on those columns can SKIP files entirely. Z-order is what enables file-skipping on multi-column filters that simple partitioning cannot provide. It only works on Delta tables (not plain parquet) because it needs the transaction log to record the optimization.
description.task: What did OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY (region, date) do, and what does it enable?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Code: spark.sql("OPTIMIZE silver.meters ZORDER BY (region, date)")

Table Size Before: 12 GB across 800 parquet files

Table Size After: 12 GB across 800 parquet files (rewritten, not recompressed)

Operation Duration: 4 minutes

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Delta transaction log entry showing OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY (region, date) operation and resulting per-file statistics

evidence.label: Plan output

fields.label: What did OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY (region, date) do, and what does it enable?
options: OPTIMIZE merged 800 small files into fewer large ones; ZORDER BY is just an alphabetization marker that has no runtime effect. The transaction log entry records the operation for time-travel only.

ZORDER physically reorganized files so rows with similar (region, date) values are co-located in the same parquet file. Per-file min/max statistics now allow Spark to skip files whose range cannot match a query's (region, date) filter.
OPTIMIZE created Z-order indexes alongside the parquet files; the indexes are read at query time to filter rows. Without ZORDER indexes, queries fall back to full-table scans on Delta tables.

ZORDER changed the table's primary key to (region, date). Future updates must use these columns; reads not filtering on (region, date) will fail with a key-mismatch error from the transaction log validator.
fields.correctAnswer: ZORDER physically reorganized files so rows with similar (region, date) values are co-located in the same parquet file. Per-file min/max statistics now allow Spark to skip files whose range cannot match a query's (region, date) filter.
fields.rationale: Multi-dimensional clustering plus per-file statistics together create the file-skipping foundation. After the OPTIMIZE, file part-00037 contains only NORTH region rows from April 1-15; file part-00038 contains NORTH from April 15-30. The min/max statistics in the transaction log enable file-skipping: a query filtering region == 'NORTH' AND date >= '2025-04-20' can rule out file 37 (max date 04-15 < query min) and rule in file 38. The result: queries read only matching files, not the full table. Z-order works on multiple columns simultaneously — partitioning would force a single column choice, but Z-order co-clusters on all listed columns.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats ZORDER as cosmetic; it physically reorganizes data.

Option C: Invents separate index files; ZORDER changes the parquet files themselves, not adds indexes.

Option D: Confuses Z-order with primary key. Z-order is a layout, not a key constraint.

tasks.pssReference: PSI2 lesson 7 (Delta Z-Ordering — semantics and the transaction log).

tasks.title: Z-Order Skipped Files — How to Read the Stats

description.context: After ZORDER, the proof that Z-order helped is in the FILE-SKIPPING METRIC. When you run a query against a Z-ordered Delta table and look at the plan or the Spark UI, you see a metric called numFilesRead vs numFilesTotal. If numFilesRead is much less than numFilesTotal, file-skipping engaged — Spark used the per-file min/max stats to rule out files that cannot match the filter. The metric is dollar-of-truth proof that Z-order is paying off; without it, you have no idea whether OPTIMIZE actually helped. A fully effective Z-order produces numFilesRead values 10-100× smaller than numFilesTotal for typical filtered queries.
description.task: What does numFilesRead: 12 out of 800 tell you?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Code: spark.read.format('delta').load('silver.meters').filter((col('region') == 'NORTH') & (col('date').between('2025-04-20', '2025-04-25'))).count()

Table Z Ordered By: (region, date)

Total Files: 800

Files Actually Read: 12

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Plan from a query against the Z-ordered NordGrid silver.meters table showing numFilesRead vs numFilesTotal

evidence.label: Plan output
evidence.content:
# Plan output (Delta Lake metrics visible)

+- HashAggregate(keys=[], functions=[count(1)])
   +- FileScan parquet silver.meters [region, date, daily_kw]
      DataFilters: [(region = NORTH), (date >= 2025-04-20), (date <= 2025-04-25)]
      ReadSchema: struct<region:string, date:date, ...>
      
      Delta scan metrics:
        numFilesTotal:    800
        numFilesRead:      12
        bytesRead:        ~180 MB (out of 12 GB total)
        filesSkippedByDataSkipping: 788

# Comparison: same query on a NON-Z-ordered version of the table
#   numFilesTotal:    800
#   numFilesRead:     800   ← every file opened
#   bytesRead:        ~12 GB
#   No file-skipping; full scan with row-level filter post-read

fields.label: What does numFilesRead: 12 out of 800 tell you?
options: Z-order reduced the file count from 800 to 12 during OPTIMIZE; the table now physically has only 12 files. numFilesTotal still says 800 because that count is cached from before OPTIMIZE. Refresh metadata to update.

Z-order randomly sampled 12 of 800 files for an approximate count; the result is statistical, not exact. To get exact counts on Z-ordered tables, set spark.sql.zorder.exactCount=true to disable sampling.
12 files is the bucketing output (50/4 ≈ 12 buckets matching the filter); the table was bucketed not Z-ordered. The 'numFilesRead' metric is misnamed; it actually counts buckets read at scan time.

Z-order skipped 788 files because their per-file min/max stats ruled them out for the (region, date) range filter. Only 12 files had stats overlapping the query range; Spark read those and applied the filter at row level.
fields.correctAnswer: Z-order skipped 788 files because their per-file min/max stats ruled them out for the (region, date) range filter. Only 12 files had stats overlapping the query range; Spark read those and applied the filter at row level.
fields.rationale: Z-order's payoff is file-skipping at query time. The 800 total files each have min/max statistics for region and date (recorded by OPTIMIZE in the transaction log). Spark evaluates the query's filter against each file's stats: if the filter's range cannot overlap the file's range (e.g., file's max date is 04-19 but query needs >= 04-20), Spark skips that file entirely without opening it. Here 788 files were ruled out, 12 opened. Bytes-read dropped from 12 GB to 180 MB — a 67× reduction. The 'filesSkippedByDataSkipping: 788' metric explicitly reports the count. This file-skipping is what makes Z-order valuable: simple partitioning could not have done this on (region, date) jointly without producing too many partition directories.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats OPTIMIZE as compacting to 12 files; it rewrites all 800 files clustered by Z-order.

Option B: Invents a sampling mechanism; Z-order is exact, not statistical.

Option C: Conflates Z-order with bucketing; numFilesRead is a real Delta metric.

tasks.pssReference: PSI2 lesson 7 (Delta Z-Ordering — file-skipping mechanics and metrics).

description.context: Z-order only helps queries that filter on the Z-ordered columns. If the engineer ran OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY (customer_id) but their queries filter on (region, date), the Z-order does NOTHING — there are no min/max stats on (region, date) to enable file-skipping. The plan's diagnostic: numFilesRead == numFilesTotal, even though OPTIMIZE was run recently and the team thinks Z-order is helping. This is a recognition failure mode common in Mid-level pipelines: someone runs OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY against the wrong column because they don't know which queries will hit the table later, or because they Z-ordered against an old query pattern that has since changed.

fields.label: Why is file-skipping not engaging despite a recent OPTIMIZE, and what is the fix?
options: OPTIMIZE was run against the table but Z-order skipping requires query rewrite; the engineer must add a hint /*+ DATA_SKIPPING */ to enable it. Fix: add the hint to all queries against this table.

Z-order columns and query filter columns don't match. Z-order on customer_id provides min/max stats on customer_id — useless for queries filtering region/date. Fix: re-run OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY (region, date) to match actual query patterns.
OPTIMIZE was too recent (3 hours); Z-order takes ~24 hours to propagate stats through the transaction log to the query planner. Fix: wait for stats propagation OR run REFRESH TABLE silver.meters.

Z-order requires bucketing first; the table is Z-ordered without being bucketed, which Spark silently treats as a no-op. Fix: rewrite the table with bucketBy(50, 'customer_id') BEFORE running OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY.
fields.correctAnswer: Z-order columns and query filter columns don't match. Z-order on customer_id provides min/max stats on customer_id — useless for queries filtering region/date. Fix: re-run OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY (region, date) to match actual query patterns.
fields.rationale: Statistics generated by OPTIMIZE only cover the columns named in the ZORDER BY clause. ZORDER BY (customer_id) creates customer_id stats; queries filtering customer_id can skip files. But this query filters region and date — neither has any Z-order-derived min/max stats. Result: no file-skipping possible, full table scan. The fix matches the layout to the queries: run OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY (region, date). Picking the right Z-order columns requires knowing the production query mix. If queries vary, Z-order on the most common filter columns first; if multiple filter patterns exist, Z-order can include up to ~3 columns but the early ones in the list dominate the locality.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Invents a hint requirement; Delta data-skipping is automatic when stats exist.

Option C: Invents a propagation delay; OPTIMIZE commits stats atomically with the transaction.

Option D: Conflates Z-order with bucketing prerequisites; they are independent layouts.

tasks.title: Bucketing Without OPTIMIZE — Stale File Layout

description.context: Bucketing is a WRITE-TIME optimization, but it can drift over time. A bucketed table that is appended to (not rewritten) accumulates new files that are NOT bucket-aligned with the original layout. After enough appends, the table effectively has 'old buckets + new chunks' — and Spark's query optimizer cannot use the bucket spec for shuffle skip because not all files conform to it. The diagnostic signal: BucketedTableScan in the plan but with SelectedBucketsCount: 0 out of 50 (or some other partial number), AND Exchange operators reappearing on the bucketed side. The fix is to rewrite the table periodically — INSERT OVERWRITE bucketed table SELECT * FROM bucketed table — to re-apply the bucket layout to all data.
description.task: Why did Spark refuse to use the bucket spec, and what is the fix?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Table: positions_bucketed (bucketBy(50, 'customer_id'), originally written 3 weeks ago)

Append Pattern: daily INSERT INTO without OVERWRITE

Current State: 50 original bucket files + 21 daily append files (no bucket alignment)

Engineer Assumption: bucketing still works because metadata says 50 buckets

Actual Observation: Exchange reappeared on the bucketed side

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Plan against a bucketed table that has had 3 weeks of daily appends without rewrite — bucketing has drifted, shuffle reappears

evidence.label: Plan output
evidence.content:
# Catalog metadata (still records the bucket spec)
DESCRIBE EXTENDED positions_bucketed
  Num Buckets: 50
  Bucket Columns: [customer_id]

# Actual file layout
$ ls /warehouse/positions_bucketed/
  part-00000-bucketed-c000.parquet  (3.6 MB)   ← original 50 bucket files
  part-00001-bucketed-c000.parquet
  ...
  part-00049-bucketed-c000.parquet
  part-00000-append-2025-04-14.parquet  ← 21 daily appends (NOT bucket-aligned)
  part-00000-append-2025-04-15.parquet
  ...
  part-00000-append-2025-05-04.parquet

# Plan for: positions_bucketed.join(customer_dim_bucketed_50, on='customer_id')

+- SortMergeJoin [customer_id], [customer_id], Inner
   :- Sort [customer_id ASC]
   :  +- Exchange hashpartitioning(customer_id, 50)   ← REAPPEARED!
   :     +- FileScan parquet positions_bucketed
   :        SelectedBucketsCount: 0 out of 50
   :        Bucketed: false   ← Spark refused to honor the bucket spec
   +- (other side, normally bucketed)

fields.label: Why did Spark refuse to use the bucket spec, and what is the fix?
options: The 21 daily append files are not bucket-aligned (they were written without bucketBy). Spark sees the mixed layout and refuses to honor the bucket spec. Fix: INSERT OVERWRITE the table to rewrite all files with bucket alignment.

The Exchange is a misreading of the plan; it's actually a no-op operator that AQE inserts and removes at runtime. SelectedBucketsCount: 0 means 'all 50 selected without filter' (not 'zero selected'). Fix: nothing — bucketing is working.

DELTA tables don't support bucketing; this is a Delta table that lost its bucket metadata during the last transaction log compaction. Fix: convert the table back to plain parquet to restore bucket support.

Catalyst auto-disabled bucketing for tables over 1 month old; Spark prevents stale bucket layouts from misleading the optimizer. Fix: ALTER TABLE ... SET TBLPROPERTIES ('spark.bucket.refresh'='true') to re-enable.
fields.correctAnswer: The 21 daily append files are not bucket-aligned (they were written without bucketBy). Spark sees the mixed layout and refuses to honor the bucket spec. Fix: INSERT OVERWRITE the table to rewrite all files with bucket alignment.
fields.rationale: Bucketing's correctness depends on every file conforming to the bucket layout. The original 50 bucket files were written by Spark with bucket-aware partitioning. The 21 append files were written via plain INSERT INTO, so their customer_ids are scattered across all 50 hash buckets. Spark's optimizer detects the mismatch and silently disables bucket-skip — Bucketed: false. The fix: INSERT OVERWRITE forces a full rewrite that re-aligns ALL files. Best practice: rewrite bucketed tables on a schedule, or use Delta's MERGE which preserves bucket layout.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Misreads SelectedBucketsCount: 0; that explicitly means zero buckets used.

Option C: Conflates bucketing with Delta. Bucketing works on plain parquet.

Option D: Invents a 1-month timeout; bucketing has no automatic expiry.

tasks.pssReference: PSI2 lesson 6 (Bucketing — append-time drift and refresh requirements).

tasks.title: Audit a Mid-Layout Pipeline

description.context: A NordGrid Mid engineer claims they layout-tuned a daily-billing pipeline with partitioning, bucketing, AND Z-ordering. They show the senior the table layouts AND the resulting plan and ask for review. The senior asks the engineer to verify EACH layout decision by reading the plan — not by trusting the metadata. Five sub-questions audit five different layout claims.
description.task: Read the artifact above, then answer the questions in order.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: 50-line layout-aware NordGrid pipeline; verify each layout intervention against the plan

evidence.label: Plan output
evidence.content:
# Layout setup (NordGrid silver layer)

# Table: silver.meters
#   Format: delta
#   partitionBy: (date)              ← 30 daily partitions for April 2025
#   Z-Order:    (region, customer_type)
#   Last OPTIMIZE: 2025-05-04 02:00 (today, 4 hours ago)

# Table: silver.customer_dim_bucketed
#   Format: parquet
#   bucketBy(50, 'customer_id') sortBy('customer_id')

# Pipeline code
result = (spark.read.format('delta').load('silver.meters')
    .filter((col('date').between('2025-04-01', '2025-04-30')) & (col('region') == 'NORTH'))
    .join(spark.table('silver.customer_dim_bucketed'), on='customer_id', how='inner')
    .groupBy('customer_type')
    .agg(sum('daily_kw').alias('total_kw')))
result.collect()
result.explain()

# Plan output (post-execution)
+- HashAggregate(keys=[customer_type], functions=[sum(daily_kw)])
   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(customer_type, 50)
      +- HashAggregate(keys=[customer_type], functions=[partial_sum(daily_kw)])
         +- Project [customer_type, daily_kw]
            +- ShuffledHashJoin [customer_id], [customer_id], Inner, BuildRight
               :- Exchange hashpartitioning(customer_id, 50)
               :  +- FileScan delta silver.meters
               :     PartitionFilters: [(date >= 2025-04-01), (date <= 2025-04-30)]
               :     PartitionCount: 30
               :     numFilesTotal: 240, numFilesRead: 60, filesSkippedByDataSkipping: 180
               +- FileScan parquet silver.customer_dim_bucketed
                  SelectedBucketsCount: 50 out of 50
                  Bucketed: true

fields.label: Q1 — Did partition pruning engage on silver.meters?
options: No — partition pruning failed because two filters cannot AND together at the partition layer. Region filter blocked date pruning. The 30 partition count is the table's daily-partition default, not pruned.

Partial pruning only; the date range pushed but the region filter could not because it sits outside the partition column. PartitionCount: 30 reflects date pruning alone; region filter is applied at the row level.

Yes — PartitionFilters: [(date >= 2025-04-01), (date <= 2025-04-30)] applied. PartitionCount: 30 out of ~365 yearly partitions confirms pruning to April only. Region filter is post-partition (data column).
Pruning is invisible from this output; PartitionFilters is an optimizer plan-time annotation that does not reflect runtime behavior. Read the Spark UI's stage-detail tab for actual pruning evidence.
fields.correctAnswer: Yes — PartitionFilters: [(date >= 2025-04-01), (date <= 2025-04-30)] applied. PartitionCount: 30 out of ~365 yearly partitions confirms pruning to April only. Region filter is post-partition (data column).
fields.rationale: PartitionFilters: [(date >= 2025-04-01), (date <= 2025-04-30)] confirms the date range filter applied at partition-discovery time. PartitionCount: 30 confirms 30 daily partitions were selected (the April month). The region filter is on a data column, not a partition column, so it did not contribute to partition pruning — but it appears in the FileScan's filters and is enforced at scan time. The combination works correctly: date prunes 335 partitions out of 365, leaving 30; region filter then applies via Z-order skipping (Q2).
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Invents an AND blocking rule that doesn't exist.

Option B: Treats region filter as competing with date pruning; they apply at different layers.

Option D: Treats PartitionFilters as cosmetic; it is the authoritative pruning indicator.

fields.label: Q2 — Did Z-order file-skipping engage on silver.meters?
options: File-skipping engagement cannot be determined from this metric. numFilesRead reflects task assignments to executors, not actual file skipping. Look at filesSkippedByDataSkipping in isolation: 180 is the Z-order skip count.
No — file-skipping engaged on partition pruning alone; the 60 files read correspond to the 30 partitions × 2 files each. Z-order had no effect because there's no customer_type filter in the query.

Yes — but only because OPTIMIZE was recent. Z-order data-skipping degrades within 24 hours of any append; the 4-hour-old OPTIMIZE is still effective. Tomorrow's runs of this query will see numFilesRead climb back to 240.

Yes — numFilesTotal: 240, numFilesRead: 60 means Spark skipped 180 files using Z-order min/max stats on (region, customer_type). The region filter rules out 75% of files within the 30 selected partitions.
fields.correctAnswer: Yes — numFilesTotal: 240, numFilesRead: 60 means Spark skipped 180 files using Z-order min/max stats on (region, customer_type). The region filter rules out 75% of files within the 30 selected partitions.
fields.rationale: filesSkippedByDataSkipping: 180 explicitly reports Z-order skipping. Of the 240 files within the 30 selected partitions, 180 had min/max stats on region that ruled out NORTH (only NORTH was needed); 60 files had stats overlapping NORTH and were read. Z-order on (region, customer_type) provides per-file region statistics that enable this skip. The compounded effect: partition pruning eliminates 335 partitions (date), then Z-order eliminates 180 files within the remaining 30 partitions (region). Both layouts work together.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Misreads metric definitions; numFilesRead is exactly what the name says.

Option B: Treats numFilesRead as proportional to partitions; Z-order is the explanatory factor.

Option C: Invents 24-hour Z-order decay; appends drift but stats remain valid.

fields.label: Q3 — Did bucketing eliminate a shuffle?
options: Yes, on customer_dim_bucketed only. SelectedBucketsCount: 50 of 50 confirms the bucket spec engaged. No Exchange appears above customer_dim's FileScan. silver.meters DID shuffle. One shuffle eliminated of two.
Yes, on both sides. Bucketing aligns hash distributions; both Exchanges visible in the plan are no-ops AQE inserts for stage-boundary metadata. Real runtime cost is zero shuffles for this join.

No — bucketing failed because silver.meters is not bucketed on customer_id. The customer_dim_bucketed Bucketed: true flag is metadata-only when the join partner is unbucketed. Both sides shuffled equally.
Bucketing engaged but on the wrong column — the bucket spec is for customer_id, but the groupBy is on customer_type. Partial benefit only; the post-aggregate Exchange still happens regardless.
fields.correctAnswer: Yes, on customer_dim_bucketed only. SelectedBucketsCount: 50 of 50 confirms the bucket spec engaged. No Exchange appears above customer_dim's FileScan. silver.meters DID shuffle. One shuffle eliminated of two.
fields.rationale: Single-side bucketing aligns one input to the bucket spec; the other input must shuffle separately. silver.meters is not bucketed (it's partitioned + Z-ordered, different layout), so the join needs to align — Exchange hashpartitioning(customer_id, 50) shuffles silver.meters' customer_ids to align with customer_dim's 50 buckets. ShuffledHashJoin uses the bucketed side as its hash-build; the non-bucketed side shuffles to match. Net: one shuffle eliminated (customer_dim's), one remains (silver.meters'). Better than two shuffles.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Treats Exchange as a no-op; it is a real shuffle operator.

Option C: Misreads the plan; customer_dim's bucketing engaged correctly.

Option D: Confuses join key with groupBy key; bucketing is for join, post-agg Exchange is unrelated.

fields.label: Q4 — Are the partition counts (30 partitions, 50 bucket files, 240 total files) appropriate sizes?
options: No — 50 buckets is too few for production. Production tables need at least 500 buckets for parallelism. The customer_dim's 50-bucket layout creates a parallelism bottleneck on the join phase.

No — daily partitioning is too granular; the 30 partitions for one month leave many tiny daily files. Switch to monthly partitioning (1 partition for April) and let Z-order do the work for date-range queries.
No — 50 buckets is too few for production. Production tables need at least 500 buckets for parallelism. The customer_dim's 50-bucket layout creates a parallelism bottleneck on the join phase.
Counts are roughly OK but file sizes per partition (240 files / 30 partitions = 8 files per partition) suggest a small-file issue within partitions. Run OPTIMIZE on silver.meters.
fields.correctAnswer: No — 50 buckets is too few for production. Production tables need at least 500 buckets for parallelism. The customer_dim's 50-bucket layout creates a parallelism bottleneck on the join phase.
fields.rationale: 30 daily partitions × ~400MB per partition is the canonical sweet spot. 50 bucket files of customer_dim (~3.6MB each given 200K row dim table) is small but acceptable because customer_dim itself is small and the bucket-spec metadata is what enables shuffle skip — not bucket file size. 240 total parquet files in silver.meters across 30 partitions = 8 files per partition, slightly suboptimal but within range; OPTIMIZE keeps the count from growing unbounded. Sizes are reasonable. Issues would arise only at much larger scale where OPTIMIZE frequency would need adjustment.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Invents a 500-bucket minimum; bucket count matches join partner is the rule.

Option B: Treats daily partitioning as too granular at 12GB/month scale; partition size is fine.

Option D: Treats 8 files per partition as a problem; in 100MB-1GB range, this is fine.

fields.label: Q5 — Would removing the Z-order be safe given this query?
options: Yes. Without Z-order all 240 files get read instead of 60. That is 4× more data and 4× slower. Keep ZORDER on the silver table; the OPTIMIZE cost is paying off via file-skipping.

Yes — removing Z-order saves OPTIMIZE compute time AND simplifies the table. The 4-hour-old OPTIMIZE is the one that actually helped this query; future runs would degrade anyway. Net: no long-term benefit.

Removing Z-order would IMPROVE this query because Z-order forces additional file rewriting per OPTIMIZE that fragments the layout. Without Z-order, the partition scheme alone gives better stable performance.
Z-order can be removed because the partitioning scheme already provides equivalent file-skipping; the Z-order is redundant. Remove ZORDER BY clause from future OPTIMIZE runs to save compute time.
fields.correctAnswer: Yes. Without Z-order all 240 files get read instead of 60. That is 4× more data and 4× slower. Keep ZORDER on the silver table; the OPTIMIZE cost is paying off via file-skipping.
fields.rationale: Z-order's payoff for this query is the 180-file skip — without it, all 240 files would be read. Estimated impact: 60 files read × 50MB/file = 3GB read; 240 files × 50MB = 12GB read without Z-order. 4× more data to read and process. Removing Z-order trades OPTIMIZE compute (4 minutes per run) for query-time cost (multiplied across many runs of this query). For SLA-critical queries with stable filter patterns matching Z-order columns, the trade is positive. Remove Z-order only when query patterns shift away from the Z-order columns.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Treats Z-order as transient; stats persist until next append/rewrite.

Option C: Treats Z-order as harmful to layout; it improves data skipping.

Option D: Treats partitioning as substituting for Z-order on a different column; (date) partition cannot prune by region.

tasks.pssReference: PSI2 lessons 5-7 (Partitioning, Bucketing, Z-Ordering — combined synthesis).

tasks.title: Five Missed Layout Opportunities

description.context: Final SLI exercise. A NordGrid pipeline runs correctly but is suboptimal at the layout level. The senior asks the engineer to read the layout AND the plan and identify FIVE missed layout opportunities. Each one is a different category: missed partition pruning, wrong bucket column, missing Z-order on hot column, small-file aggregation needed, OPTIMIZE not scheduled. The plan tells the story; the table layouts look fine on their own but together miss several wins.
description.task: Read the artifact above, then answer the questions in order.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: 55-line NordGrid pipeline with 5 embedded missed layout-level opportunities

evidence.label: Plan output
evidence.content:
# Layout setup

# Table: bronze.events_log (parquet, NOT partitioned, NOT bucketed)
#   Total: 8M rows / 4.2 GB across 12 files of ~350MB each
#   Schema: event_id, customer_id, event_date, event_type, kw_delta

# Table: bronze.customer_dim (parquet, bucketBy(50, 'customer_type'))
#   Total: 200K rows / 8 MB
#   Schema: customer_id, customer_type, region, signup_date

# Table: bronze.regional_dim (delta, NO ZORDER, last OPTIMIZE 6 weeks ago)
#   Total: 30 rows / 4 KB
#   Schema: region_code, region_name, capacity_mw

# Pipeline code
result = (spark.read.parquet('bronze/events_log/')
    .filter(col('event_date') == '2025-04-30')
    .join(spark.table('bronze.customer_dim'), on='customer_id', how='inner')
    .join(spark.read.format('delta').load('bronze/regional_dim/'), on='region', how='inner')
    .groupBy('customer_type', 'region_name')
    .agg(sum('kw_delta').alias('total_kw')))
result.collect()
result.explain()

# Plan output (post-execution)
+- HashAggregate(keys=[customer_type, region_name], functions=[sum(kw_delta)])
   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(customer_type, region_name, 200)
      +- HashAggregate(keys=[customer_type, region_name], functions=[partial_sum(kw_delta)])
         +- BroadcastHashJoin [region], [region_code], Inner, BuildRight
            :- ShuffledHashJoin [customer_id], [customer_id], Inner, BuildRight
            :   :- Exchange hashpartitioning(customer_id, 50)
            :   :  +- Filter (event_date = 2025-04-30)
            :   :     +- FileScan parquet bronze.events_log
            :   :        PartitionFilters: []         ← no pruning
            :   :        PushedFilters: [EqualTo(event_date, 2025-04-30)]
            :   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(customer_id, 50)   ← second shuffle
            :      +- FileScan parquet bronze.customer_dim
            :         SelectedBucketsCount: 0 out of 50         ← bucket spec ignored
            :         Bucketed: false
            +- BroadcastExchange
               +- FileScan delta bronze.regional_dim
                  numFilesTotal: 47, numFilesRead: 47   ← all files read
                  filesSkippedByDataSkipping: 0

fields.label: Q1 — Missed Opportunity #1: events_log has no partitioning, so the date filter cannot prune. What is the fix?
options: Rewrite events_log with partitionBy('event_date'). Future date-filtered queries prune to single-day directories. PartitionFilters would show the predicate; PartitionCount would drop to 1.
Add a filter rewrite hint /*+ PARTITION_PUSHDOWN */ to force pruning at the file level; without the hint, Catalyst doesn't try. No layout change is needed for this fix to work.
PushedFilters: [EqualTo(event_date, 2025-04-30)] confirms pushdown at file level — partition pruning would be redundant in this case. No fix is needed for the layout to deliver good performance.
Rewrite events_log as a Delta table with Z-ORDER BY (event_date); Z-order provides equivalent file-skipping to partitioning without the overhead of multiple directories.
fields.correctAnswer: Rewrite events_log with partitionBy('event_date'). Future date-filtered queries prune to single-day directories. PartitionFilters would show the predicate; PartitionCount would drop to 1.
fields.rationale: events_log has no partition columns (PartitionFilters: []), so the date filter applies as PushedFilters at file level — Spark opens every parquet file but skips rows that don't match. With partitionBy('event_date'), the same query would prune to 1 directory and never open files for other dates. For 8M rows across 365 days × ~22K rows per day, this is a 365× reduction in file-open overhead and bytes read. PushedFilters helps but doesn't eliminate file opens like partitioning does.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Invents a hint mechanism; pushdown happens automatically.

Option C: Conflates pushdown with partition pruning; they operate at different layers.

Option D: Z-order on parquet doesn't exist (Delta-only); also Z-order doesn't replace partition pruning at directory level.

fields.label: Q2 — Missed Opportunity #2: customer_dim is bucketed BY customer_type but joined ON customer_id. What is the fix?
options: The bucket spec is fine; SelectedBucketsCount: 0 means 'all 50 selected without filter' (a counter-intuitive metric naming). Bucketing IS engaging on customer_type for the post-aggregate Exchange.
Add the bucket-key hint /*+ USE_BUCKETING(customer_id) */ to override the column mismatch; this lets Spark use the customer_type bucket for customer_id joins. No rewrite needed.

The bucket column doesn't match the join key; Spark cannot use the bucket spec for shuffle skip. SelectedBucketsCount: 0 confirms. Fix: rewrite customer_dim with bucketBy(50, 'customer_id') to match the actual join column.

customer_dim should not be bucketed at all because it's only 8MB; broadcast it instead. Add broadcast(customer_dim) hint to the join — broadcasting skips the shuffle entirely without needing a bucket spec at all.
fields.correctAnswer: The bucket column doesn't match the join key; Spark cannot use the bucket spec for shuffle skip. SelectedBucketsCount: 0 confirms. Fix: rewrite customer_dim with bucketBy(50, 'customer_id') to match the actual join column.
fields.rationale: Spark refuses to honor the bucket spec when the hash distribution does not align with the equality predicate at runtime. customer_dim is bucketBy('customer_type'), but the join is ON customer_id — completely different column. Spark sees the mismatch and refuses to use the bucket spec (Bucketed: false, SelectedBucketsCount: 0). Both sides shuffle. The fix is rewrite: bucketBy(50, 'customer_id'). Bucketing column should match the most common join key; if multiple join patterns exist, pick the one that benefits most.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Misreads SelectedBucketsCount: 0; that means zero, not all.

Option B: Invents a hint that overrides bucket column; not a real Spark feature.

Option D: Suggests broadcast as substitute; broadcast works here but doesn't address the bucketing-mismatch lesson.

fields.label: Q3 — Missed Opportunity #3: regional_dim is Delta but last OPTIMIZE was 6 weeks ago. What is the symptom and fix?
options: 47 files is correct because each daily append produces one tombstone file; Delta requires this for time-travel. Fix: turn off time-travel via DELETE FROM regional_dim WHERE _commit_version < (current - 7).
The 47 files reflect Delta's transaction log entries, not data files; this is normal behavior for Delta tables. No fix needed beyond regular VACUUM to clean log entries.
regional_dim being broadcast (BroadcastExchange in plan) means file count is irrelevant — the entire 4KB table is sent to every executor. No fix needed at the layout level.

regional_dim has 47 files for 30 rows of data — extreme small-file fragmentation from 6 weeks of appends without compaction. Fix: schedule OPTIMIZE bronze.regional_dim weekly; consider ZORDER BY (region_code).
fields.correctAnswer: regional_dim has 47 files for 30 rows of data — extreme small-file fragmentation from 6 weeks of appends without compaction. Fix: schedule OPTIMIZE bronze.regional_dim weekly; consider ZORDER BY (region_code).
fields.rationale: 47 data files for a 4KB table is an extreme small-file scenario — every daily append created another file without compaction. Each file has parquet footer overhead (~1KB). Reading 47 files × 1KB footer = 47KB of metadata for 4KB of actual data. The plan also shows numFilesRead: 47 with filesSkippedByDataSkipping: 0 — no Z-order means no skipping. The fix has two parts: schedule OPTIMIZE weekly to compact files (47 → 1-2 files) and add ZORDER BY (region_code) for queries filtering by region. Even small Delta tables need OPTIMIZE.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Invents a tombstone-per-append mechanism; Delta uses MERGE-style log entries.

Option B: Conflates data files with transaction log entries; numFilesTotal is data files.

Option C: Treats broadcast as making file count irrelevant; broadcast still reads the source.

fields.label: Q4 — Missed Opportunity #4: The events_log filter event_date == '2025-04-30' is followed by a join on customer_id. Even after partition pruning fix (Q1), the join still shuffles. Is there a layout fix?
options: Yes — disable bucketing entirely; convert customer_dim to broadcast (it's only 8MB). Broadcasting eliminates the shuffle without the complexity of bucket alignment.
No — once partition pruning fires, bucketing becomes irrelevant. The pruned partition is small enough that shuffle cost is negligible compared to scan time.
Yes — bucket events_log by customer_id at write time. With customer_dim also bucketBy(50, 'customer_id'), both sides match. The join shuffle disappears entirely. Layout composes both.
Yes — but partitioning + bucketing on the same table is forbidden in plain parquet. Convert events_log to Delta first, then partition AND bucket the new table.
fields.correctAnswer: Yes — bucket events_log by customer_id at write time. With customer_dim also bucketBy(50, 'customer_id'), both sides match. The join shuffle disappears entirely. Layout composes both.
fields.rationale: Partitioning and bucketing compose. partitionBy('event_date') prunes which directories to read; within each directory, bucketBy(50, 'customer_id') ensures customer_id rows are pre-distributed. Combined with customer_dim's customer_id bucketing (Q2 fix), BOTH sides of the join have matching 50-bucket layouts and Spark eliminates BOTH shuffles. The layout: events_log partitionBy('event_date').bucketBy(50, 'customer_id') is a common production pattern. Plain parquet supports it; Delta supports it too. The two optimizations are orthogonal — directory-level pruning and within-directory bucket alignment.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Suggests broadcast over bucket; broadcast works at small dim scale, but bucketing is the layout lesson.

Option B: Treats partition pruning as making bucketing redundant; they save different costs.

Option D: Invents a no-combine restriction in plain parquet; partition+bucket combines fine.

fields.label: Q5 — Missed Opportunity #5: Looking at all four fixes together (Q1-Q4), which would have the LARGEST impact on this query's runtime?
options: Q3 fix (OPTIMIZE regional_dim) — reading 47 small files instead of 1 dominates runtime even though regional_dim is tiny. Compaction yields the biggest single improvement.
Q1 fix (partition events_log by event_date) — events_log is 4.2GB, the biggest table by far. Pruning to 1 day's data (~140MB) is a 30× reduction in bytes read. This dwarfs the other fixes' impact.
Q2 fix (re-bucket customer_dim by customer_id) — bucket-shuffle elimination is the largest possible single improvement because it removes a cluster-wide data movement step entirely.
Q4 fix (bucket events_log too) — eliminating BOTH sides of the join shuffle eliminates the largest cost in the plan. Bigger win than any individual layout change.
fields.correctAnswer: Q1 fix (partition events_log by event_date) — events_log is 4.2GB, the biggest table by far. Pruning to 1 day's data (~140MB) is a 30× reduction in bytes read. This dwarfs the other fixes' impact.
fields.rationale: Quantitative ranking: Q1 prunes 4.2GB → ~140MB (30× reduction in bytes read). Q4 (combined with Q2) saves the larger join shuffle but only on 140MB after Q1 pruning — Q4's gain is conditional on Q1 having fired. Q3 fixes 47 files of 4KB total — small absolute impact even though percentage-wise huge. Q2 alone (without Q4) saves one shuffle on a 4.2GB-scale operation. Q1's partition pruning at the source is the largest single improvement; downstream optimizations compound off that base. Rule: optimize the layer with the most data first.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Overweights file count vs data volume; 47 small files have small absolute cost.

Option C: Overweights shuffle elimination vs source-side data reduction.

Option D: Conditional gain (depends on Q1) is smaller than Q1 itself.

tasks.pssReference: PSI2 lessons 5-7 (Storage Layout — multi-table layout interactions and prioritization).
